title: Tamsin and the Cellar
premise: Ansel Nystrom returns to the decaying family house in Hollowmere to bury his twin sister Tamsin, only to find the death certificate lists him instead. The village remembers a bargain struck in 1974, when their grandmother took something from the cellar—a child's name, carved into a bell that was melted down but never silenced. As frost creeps inward from the walls and the ghost-bell tolls each night closer to the house, Ansel learns the cellar keeps whoever the bell names. To survive, he must descend, return what was taken, and choose between the duty of dying in Tamsin's place and the love of the found family—the village outcasts—who refuse to let him go. In the end, Ansel gives the bell back its name rather than his own, freeing both twins: Tamsin is buried as herself, and Ansel walks out of Hollowmere alive but forever able to hear bells no one else can.
about_author: Juniper Okafor is a former church archivist who grew up in a coastal village where three parishes claim to own the same missing bell. She writes horror about houses that keep receipts, and lives with her partner and an elderly dog named Vesper.

chapters.title: The Wrong Sibling
chapters.summary: Ansel arrives in Hollowmere by night bus with Tamsin's ashes, POV his. At the funeral home, the paperwork reads 'Ansel Nystrom, deceased.' He assumes clerical error, but the undertaker crosses herself. Emotional beat: disorientation sharpening into dread as home curdles into something watched.

chapters.title: Nystrom House Keeps Its Own Hours
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV settling into the inherited house; doors he doesn't open are open, and frost ferns grow on the inside of windows despite mild weather. A neighbor, Idris Vale, warns him not to answer anything that knocks before dawn. Beat: uneasy domesticity, the first rule given.

chapters.title: What the Bell Was
chapters.summary: In the village archive, Ansel finds photos of St. Brannoc's bell, melted down in 1911—yet parish records list it as 'on loan' until 1974, when his grandmother signed something. POV alternates with archival documents. Beat: curiosity becoming complicity; he realizes his family's name is on the debt.

chapters.title: First Tolling
chapters.summary: Ansel wakes at 3:11 a.m. to a bell tolling from the direction of the roofless church. No bell exists there. The frost on his bedroom window has formed a pattern like sound waves. Beat: denial cracking; the noises he's explained for twenty years were rehearsals.

chapters.title: The Outcasts of Hollowmere
chapters.summary: Idris introduces Ansel to the village's overlooked: Wren, a teenage bell-historian; Maud, who went deaf the year of the last tolling; and Sam, the gravedigger who never buries anyone before checking the ground first. Found family forms over bad tea. Beat: warmth against isolation; Ansel stops being invisible.

chapters.title: Tamsin's Room
chapters.summary: Ansel finally opens his twin's sealed childhood room and finds her diaries: she heard the bell too, all her life, and came back to Hollowmere alone two weeks before her death. Her last entry: 'It wants the one whose name is written twice.' Beat: grief weaponized; guilt that she faced it alone.

chapters.title: The 1974 Ledger
chapters.summary: Maud, reading lips through the floorboards as a girl, recalls the night Ansel's grandmother descended the cellar stairs carrying the bell's clapper wrapped in cloth—and came up without it, or without something else. POV Maud's memory interleaved with Ansel's present. Beat: the shape of the theft emerges.

chapters.title: Frost Writes Its Pattern
chapters.summary: The frost inside the house now spells letters overnight: ANSEL, then TAM SIN crossed out, then ANSEL again. The bell tolls twice nightly. Villagers begin avoiding the Nystrom gate. Beat: escalation; the house is choosing, and the deadline becomes visible.

chapters.title: Down the Cellar Stairs (Not Yet)
chapters.summary: Ansel descends as far as the landing; below, cold like deep water and a sound like a name being pronounced very slowly. He retreats when his own voice answers him from the dark. Beat: terror and temptation braided—the cellar knows him intimately.

chapters.title: Wren's Theory of Bells
chapters.summary: Wren explains: a bell holds the name of whoever paid for its silence; melt the metal, keep the name. The 1974 ledger shows grandmother bought the village's safety with a Nystrom name—Tamsin's, pre-written at birth. Beat: intellectual horror; the inheritance was always a sentence.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: Ansel tells the outcasts he'll go down and take Tamsin's place properly—die as himself so the pattern closes. Idris, quietly furious, says duty is just fear wearing its Sunday clothes. First kiss between Ansel and Idris, interrupted by thirteen tolls. Beat: tenderness against fatalism; stakes become personal.

chapters.title: The Village That Forgot on Purpose
chapters.summary: Ansel confronts the parish council, who admit they've known since 1974 and let the Nystroms 'keep to themselves' because forgetting was the price of peace. POV shifts briefly to the council chair's shame. Beat: betrayal; the found family is the only honest thing left.

chapters.title: Sam Digs Early
chapters.summary: Sam opens Tamsin's grave plot and finds it already occupied by a coffin bearing Ansel's name, dated twenty years ago—the year the noises started. Beat: retroactive horror; Ansel has been dead on paper since adolescence, and the cellar has been patient.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Letter
chapters.summary: Behind the cellar landing's loose brick, Ansel finds his grandmother's confession: she didn't steal the clapper—she stole the naming right, hoping to spare her grandchildren, and failed. 'Return what was taken' means giving the bell back its voice, not a body. Beat: the rules invert; hope enters.

chapters.title: Thirteen Nights
chapters.summary: A countdown structure: thirteen chapters compressed into one, each night the frost reaches one room deeper and the tolling comes one hour earlier. The outcasts take shifts keeping watch, singing off-key to drown the bell. Beat: siege intimacy; love practiced as logistics.

chapters.title: Maud Hears It Again
chapters.summary: On the final night, Maud's deafness breaks—she hears the bell and weeps, because it means the end is close enough to touch. She gives Ansel the clapper's hiding place she's kept silent for fifty years. Beat: sacrifice of long-held protection; the old wound reopens willingly.

chapters.title: Descent
chapters.summary: Ansel goes down with the clapper, Wren's research notes, and Idris's hand in his until the stairs turn. The cellar is the church that was never built, pews of ice, and the bell hanging whole and un-melted, humming his name. Beat: threshold crossing; awe and terror fused.

chapters.title: The Naming
chapters.summary: Climax part one: the bell demands a name to ring forever. Ansel offers his own; the frost accepts—then he speaks the bell's true name, recovered by Wren from the 1911 founder's mark, and hangs the clapper himself. Beat: the trick of returning rather than replacing.

chapters.title: What the Bell Rings For
chapters.summary: Climax part two: the bell tolls once, freely, and every frozen thing in the house thaws at once. The coffin in Tamsin's plot crumbles to leaf mold. But the bell, freed, asks its price of Ansel: he will hear it, always, everywhere. Beat: victory with a scar; magic keeps its receipt.

chapters.title: Burial, Correctly Addressed
chapters.summary: Tamsin is buried under her own name with the whole strange congregation of outcasts attending. Ansel reads her diaries aloud, finishing the sentences she left unfinished. Beat: grief resolved into ceremony; the wrong sibling righted at last.

chapters.title: Staying Visible
chapters.summary: Ansel chooses to stay in Hollowmere—not trapped now, but kept: Idris's garden, Wren's archive, Maud's kitchen. The house's frost forms, once, a single word: STAY. He does. Beat: found family chosen over escape; haunting turned homely.

chapters.title: Coda: The Man Who Hears Bells
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Ansel's POV years later: travelers report a bell ringing in villages with no bells, always kindly, always pointing lost people home. Ansel smiles, pours tea for the outcasts, and listens. Beat: quiet wonder; the inheritance transformed from curse to gift.
